q: A small SOC has no tiers: every analyst takes alerts from one shared queue and follows each as far as it goes. One analyst picks up an alert that turns out to be a genuine intrusion and works it for the rest of the shift. Which structural weakness does this expose most directly?
options: The queue stops moving, so other alerts, possibly more urgent ones, wait unseen
Handling becomes inconsistent, because each analyst sets their own depth of checks
Specialist expertise is wasted on closing alerts from misconfigured backup jobs
The feedback loop to detection rules breaks, because nobody files tuning requests
explanation: While one analyst is rightly absorbed by a deep case, the alerts they would have triaged sit untouched; tiers separate breadth from depth to stop this. Inconsistency is a real weakness of the flat model too, but it is not what this scenario shows.

q: A Tier 1 analyst has used the full time budget on an alert. The evidence neither clearly meets the playbook's escalation criteria nor supports a benign explanation. What is the correct action?
options: Keep investigating past the budget until the evidence becomes conclusive
Close it as a false positive, since the escalation criteria were not clearly met
Escalate it as inconclusive, with notes on what was checked and ruled out
Close it as a benign true positive and ask the rule owner to review it later
explanation: The time budget is a ceiling that triggers escalation; an undecided case goes up as inconclusive with notes, which protects both the queue and the case. Closing it as a false positive without evidence risks hiding a real intrusion.

q: A rule for mass file modification fires on a file server during a scheduled data migration, and the analyst finds an approved change ticket covering exactly that host and time window. How should the alert be closed?
options: As a false positive, with a request to detection engineering to rewrite the rule
As a benign true positive, citing the change ticket as the reason
As a true positive, escalated to Tier 2 so the migration can be scoped
As inconclusive, because a change ticket alone does not prove intent
explanation: The rule correctly detected the activity it was designed for, and the activity was authorised, so it is a benign true positive with the ticket cited. A false positive would mean the rule matched something it was not meant to match, which is not the case here.

q: A rule meant to detect a script interpreter launched by an Office application keeps firing when a document-conversion service starts a print driver helper, which is not a script interpreter at all. Besides closing each alert, what should the Tier 1 analyst produce?
options: An escalation to Tier 2, since repeated alerts on one service suggest compromise
A benign true positive record citing the conversion service's change history
A permanent personal note so future shifts recognise and close it quickly
A false-positive disposition plus a tuning request routed to the rule's owner
explanation: The rule's logic matched something it was not designed to catch, which is a false positive; the closure should feed detection engineering so the rule is fixed. It is not a benign true positive, because the detected behaviour is not what the rule targets.

q: In the lab triage output, six of the seven alerts (log cleared, Office spawning a script, two new local admins, a large upload, a regular small beacon) concern host WS-104. What should a disciplined Tier 1 analyst do with them?
options: Work them as six separate tickets in descending order of priority score
Escalate only the log-cleared alert, since it has the highest score
Link them into one case and escalate it as a probable incident
Close the low-scoring beacon alert first to shorten the queue quickly
explanation: Together the alerts describe a sequence on one host that none proves alone, so they belong in one case escalated as a probable incident. Escalating only the top alert would leave Tier 2 without the context that makes the case convincing.

q: In the lab's triage.py, the R5 log-cleared alert on WS-104 scores 10.8 while the R6 beacon alert on the same host scores 3.6. Which inputs produce this difference?
options: Rule base severity multiplied by rule confidence and by asset criticality
The number of events matched multiplied by the age of the newest event
Threat-intelligence reputation of the source IP added to user privilege
The analyst's manual severity rating averaged with the SIEM default
explanation: triage.py defines priority as base severity times confidence times asset criticality; the host is the same, so the difference comes from the rules' severity and confidence. Source-IP reputation is not part of the formula, and both lines show ip=n/a.

q: The lab queue contains an R2 alert (many users failed from one external address, then one succeeded) for host WS-107 and user gopal. Why should it be a separate case from the WS-104 alerts?
options: Because its priority score of 7.2 is too low to be grouped with the 10.8 alert
Because VPN alerts are always handled by the identity team, not by the SOC
Because it came from the VPN source, and cases must not mix log sources
Because it concerns a different host and user and a distinct attack pattern
explanation: Cases group alerts that describe the same activity; R2 involves another host, another user and a password-spraying pattern unrelated to the WS-104 sequence. Mixing log sources within a case is normal, so the source is not the reason.

q: At 03:00 the EDR raises a high-confidence ransomware detection on a branch workstation. The playbook pre-authorises endpoint isolation for this detection. What should the Tier 1 analyst on shift do?
options: Record the alert and leave it for the morning shift's Tier 2 analysts
Isolate the endpoint through the EDR and escalate via the on-call path
Shut down the file server the workstation maps, to stop encryption spreading
Message a Tier 2 colleague on chat and wait for an answer before acting
explanation: Pre-authorised, reversible first-response actions exist so containment does not wait while an attack spreads; the case then goes up through the on-call path. Shutting down a server is outside the pre-agreed action and could cause more harm than the attacker.

q: A playbook says suspicious-encryption alerts should be escalated 'during business hours'. At 03:00 an analyst sees evidence strongly suggesting ransomware. What is the correct course?
options: Escalate through the emergency on-call path, document why, then request a playbook change
Follow the playbook literally and escalate at 09:00, noting the delay in the case
Close the alert as inconclusive, since the playbook does not cover this situation
Wait for a second alert to confirm before deviating from the written playbook
explanation: Playbooks support judgement but must not block urgent action; when they conflict with the evidence, the analyst escalates, records the reason and asks for the playbook to be fixed. Waiting until 09:00 could let encryption spread and use up a reporting window.

q: Why are the first-response actions a SOC is allowed to take without further approval deliberately kept limited and reversible?
options: Because EDR tools cannot technically perform irreversible actions on endpoints
Because regulators forbid SOC analysts from changing production systems at all
So they can be agreed with system owners in advance and used without waiting
So Tier 1 can avoid documenting them in the case-management system
explanation: Limited, reversible actions such as isolating an endpoint can be pre-agreed with system owners, which lets the SOC act immediately while keeping the cost of a mistake low. Regulators do not forbid such actions, and every action must still be documented.

q: An escalated case lands with an analyst who must build a timeline, find every affected host and account, and agree which accounts to disable with the identity team. Which tier's work is this, and what question does it answer?
options: Tier 1: is the alert real, and is there an obvious benign explanation?
Tier 2: what exactly happened, how far does it reach, and what must be done?
Tier 3: which attacker activity exists that no rule has alerted on yet?
SOC lead: which metrics and stakeholders should hear about this case?
explanation: Scoping, root cause and containment recommendations coordinated with IT are Tier 2 investigation work. Tier 1 asks whether the alert is real; hypothesis-driven searching for unalerted activity is Tier 3 hunting.

q: For months, Tier 1 has closed the same alert caused by a legitimate backup tool as a false positive several times a day, yet the rule has never changed. Which part of the SOC structure is failing?
options: The escalation path from Tier 1 to Tier 2 for probable true positives
The Tier 1 time budget, which is too generous for this alert type
The SOC lead's oversight of case ownership in case management
The feedback flow from closures and investigations back to the rules
explanation: Knowledge should flow back down from closures and investigations into rule and playbook changes; without that feedback the same false positives reach Tier 1 every day. The escalation path is irrelevant because these alerts are correctly closed, not escalated.

q: A Tier 1 analyst sends a chat message to a Tier 2 colleague saying 'have a look at WS-104' and returns to the queue. Why is this an unsafe way to escalate?
options: No owner is recorded in case management, so the case can be lost, especially at shift change
Chat messages cannot carry screenshots, so the evidence is always lost in transit
Tier 2 analysts are not permitted to accept work from Tier 1 outside office hours
It breaches the CERT-In requirement that every escalation be reported within six hours
explanation: Escalation must happen in the case-management system with an acknowledgement, so ownership is recorded; a chat message to someone who has gone home leaves the case with no owner. CERT-In's six-hour rule concerns reporting incidents, not internal escalations.

q: The same suspicious-PowerShell rule fires on a test virtual machine and on a domain controller within the same minute. Why should the analyst escalate the domain-controller alert faster?
options: Because domain controllers produce fewer false positives than other hosts
Because test machines are outside the SOC's monitoring scope by default
Because asset criticality is an escalation factor, so impact there is higher
Because the second alert to arrive is always the more reliable one
explanation: Escalation criteria combine evidence strength with asset and identity criticality; the same evidence on a domain controller carries far greater potential impact. This is why CMDB enrichment is a Tier 1 task. Test machines are still monitored.

q: Which escalation note gives Tier 2 the most useful starting point?
options: Looks suspicious on WS-104, several alerts fired overnight, please check urgently
R5 fired on WS-104 at high severity; escalating per playbook, priority 10.8
WS-104 might be compromised; user divya is a payments approver so treat as critical
Log cleared on WS-104 after new admins and a large upload; no change ticket found; meets critical-asset criteria
explanation: A good escalation states what was observed, what was checked, what was ruled out and why the criteria were met, so Tier 2 does not redo Tier 1's work. The other notes either give no evidence or give a score without the checks behind it.

q: A SOC treats an alert on a reception kiosk and one on the payments server with equal urgency because it has no record of what either system is. Under the NIST CSF 2.0, which Function's weakness is causing this?
options: Protect, because the kiosk should have been hardened before going live
Identify, because the asset inventory and criticality context are missing
Respond, because the containment playbooks have not been written yet
Recover, because the backup priorities of each system are undefined
explanation: The SOC lives mainly in Detect and Respond but depends on Identify for an asset inventory that says which systems matter most. Hardening (Protect) affects what happens, not how the SOC prioritises alerts it receives.

q: A covered entity in India has no out-of-hours escalation path; critical alerts raised overnight are read by the morning shift. How does the CERT-In Direction of 28 April 2022 make this especially risky?
options: Reporting is required within six hours of noticing, so an overnight wait may use up the window
Logs must be kept for 180 days, so overnight alerts are deleted before the morning shift
CERT-In requires a 24x7 staffed SOC for every registered company in India
Incidents must be reported within 72 hours, which an overnight delay always exceeds
explanation: The Direction requires covered entities to report specified incidents within six hours of noticing them; an alert left until morning may already have consumed that window. The 180-day figure is log retention, not deletion, and 72 hours is not the CERT-In deadline.

q: A SOC manager starts rewarding Tier 1 analysts for closing alerts well inside their time budget. What risk does this create?
options: Tier 2 becomes overloaded because analysts escalate everything to save time
Real alerts get closed as false positives because speed is rewarded over accuracy
Detection engineers stop receiving alerts because rules are disabled to cut volume
Case records grow too long because analysts paste every log line into notes
explanation: The time budget is a ceiling that triggers escalation, not a target; rewarding speed pushes analysts to close cases they should escalate. Over-escalation is the opposite pressure and is not what a closure reward encourages.

q: A large tiered SOC finds that details noticed by Tier 1 are often missing by the time a case reaches Tier 3, and analysts leave after months of repetitive queue work. Which redesign addresses both problems most directly?
options: Adding a fourth tier between Tier 2 and Tier 3 to review every escalation
Raising the Tier 1 time budget so analysts can investigate each case deeper
Functional teams where one analyst owns a case end to end, with triage automated
Outsourcing Tier 1 to a provider so that internal staff only handle Tier 2 work
explanation: Functional teams keep case ownership continuous, so context survives, and automation removes repetitive triage that drives burnout. Adding another tier creates one more hand-off, which makes context loss worse.

q: Banyan Microfinance's night shift has only two analysts. How is the SOC's work best organised for that shift?
options: One analyst acts as Tier 1 and the other as Tier 2, with Tier 3 left vacant
Both analysts triage only and leave every escalated case for the day shift
All alerts are queued unread overnight and triaged together each morning
Both analysts triage, either takes a case to closure, and on-call Tier 3 is paged
explanation: A two-person shift cannot run three tiers, so it uses a functional model: both triage, either can own a case through to closure, and a specialist is paged when forensics are needed. Leaving cases for the day shift recreates the overnight gap.

q: After automating most enrichment in a SOAR platform and abolishing the 'Tier 1' job title, a SOC manager proposes deleting the written escalation criteria. Why is this a mistake?
options: Someone still makes the first close-or-escalate decision on each alert and needs criteria
SOAR platforms cannot run unless escalation criteria are stored in their configuration
Auditors require the tier job titles to be kept in the organisation chart
Without Tier 1, Tier 2 can no longer declare incidents under the response plan
explanation: Automation and functional teams redistribute triage work but do not remove it; whoever makes the first decision still needs written criteria. The tier vocabulary describes the work, whatever the job titles say.

q: The US Senate committee analysis of the 2013 Target breach reported that automated intrusion warnings were raised but not acted on effectively. Which control from the lesson targets that failure most directly?
options: Adding more detection rules so that the intrusion produces stronger alerts
Restricting case-system access so that only senior analysts can read alerts
Extending log retention so that evidence is available for later investigation
Automatically notifying the SOC lead and on-call staff about unacknowledged critical cases
explanation: In that case the technology detected but the organisation did not act; alerting on unacknowledged high-severity cases attacks exactly that gap. More rules would only add alerts that could also go unanswered.

q: A new SOC writes a single escalation rule for every alert type: 'escalate anything suspicious'. What outcome does the lesson predict?
options: Tier 1 closures become more accurate, because analysts escalate more often
Detection engineering receives more tuning requests and false positives fall
Overload moves up to Tier 2, or Tier 1 grows unsure and reluctant to escalate
Case volume falls, because suspicious activity is defined narrowly by the rule
explanation: Vague criteria either send everything to Tier 2, recreating the overload one level up, or leave Tier 1 uncertain and hesitant. Good criteria are written per alert type and combine evidence, criticality, time sensitivity and effort.

q: After a CERT-In advisory, an analyst searches the estate for signs of a credential-theft technique that none of the SOC's rules has ever alerted on, starting from a written hypothesis. Which function is this?
options: Detection engineering, because it involves writing and tuning new rules
Threat hunting, a proactive Tier 3 search for activity no rule has flagged
Digital forensics, because it requires preserving disk and memory evidence
Tier 2 scoping, because it builds a timeline of an escalated incident
explanation: Hypothesis-driven searching for activity that no rule has alerted on is threat hunting. Detection engineering may later turn a finding into a rule, but the search itself is the hunt; scoping applies to an already escalated case.

q: Each week a senior analyst reviews a random sample of the cases Tier 1 closed. What is the main purpose of this review?
options: To catch mis-closures and turn them into training and tuning items
To measure each analyst's closure speed for the monthly league table
To re-open every sampled case so Tier 2 can investigate it fully
To delete closed cases older than 180 days from the case system
explanation: Quality review of closures is a control protecting the tier structure: a wrong Tier 1 closure hides a case from everyone above it, so sampled mistakes become training and rule changes. Ranking by speed would encourage the hurried closures the review is meant to catch.
